entries.en: We're fugitives on the run. Very exciting, Shepard.
Your ship's amazing, Shepard. I've never seen a drive core like this before. I can't believe you were able to fit it into a ship this small.
Oh. Hello, Shepard.
Shepard. I'm glad you're here.
It feels like we're getting near the end, doesn't it, Shepard? With Saren, I mean.
Hey, Shepard. You need something?
I could get used to living like this.
I love this place -- the crowds, the action. It's great!
Why would anyone want to live here?
If my people found an uninhabited world like this, they'd just keep on looking.
I've never seen snow before. Can't say I'm impressed.
I don't like it here. Too muggy.
This place gives me the creeps.
Saren's got to be close now!
I'm here, Shepard.
Ready when you are.
With you all the way.
I want to know more about the Pilgrimage.
Tell me about your people.
I want to know more about the geth.
I should go.
Pilgrimage
Quarians
Geth
Goodbye.
I wonder what the Council would do to us if we got caught?
See you later.
I'm starting to understand why you humans have been so successful. I had no idea Alliance vessels were so advanced!
A month ago, I was patching a makeshift fuel line into a converted tug ship in the flotilla. Now I'm sitting on board one of the most advanced vessels in Citadel space.
I have to thank you again for bringing me along. Traveling on a vessel like this is a dream come true for me.
We're on the same side here. My people have more reason to hate the geth than anyone, remember?
But you can't blame me for being a little excited. I never dreamed I'd get a chance to travel on a ship as advanced as the Normandy.
It comes with being a quarian. The Migrant Fleet is the key to the survival of my people. Ships are our most valuable resource.
But we don't have anything like this. We make do with cast-offs and second-hand equipment. We just try to keep them running for as long as we can.
Some of the Fleet's larger vessels date all the way back to our original flight from the geth.
They're constantly being repaired, modified, and refitted. They aren't pretty, but they work. Mostly.
We've tried to make ourselves as independent as possible on the flotilla. Grow our own food, mine and process our own fuel.
But some things we just can't make on our own. A patch to maintain the hull integrity requires raw materials we just don't have. That's why our Pilgrimages are so important.
No problem. What do you want to talk about?
I know why I'm here. I'll do whatever I can to help you stop Saren and drive his geth armies back beyond the Veil.
Never mind. It's nothing. I'll be fine.
I don't know. Your ship is amazing, and your crew's been really great to me. Especially your chief engineer. But I just sort of feel... out of place.
The Normandy runs so smooth it feels like we're not even moving. And the engines are so quiet. How do you sleep at night?
Back on the flotilla, the last thing you want to hear is silence. It means an engine's died or an air filter's shut down.
I guess you don't have to worry about that here, but old habits die hard.
But it's more than just the silence. This ship feels so empty; it's like half the crew is missing.
Back home, I couldn't wait to go on my Pilgrimage. I couldn't wait to get away from the crowds. Now that I'm out here, I kind of miss them.
Don't worry. Like I said, it's nothing. I'll be there when you need me.
The Normandy's a prototype. Cutting edge technology.
I don't like the idea of aliens studying the architecture of Alliance ships.
I had no idea you found ship technology so interesting.
I can't believe your fleet's still using ships that are three centuries old.
I want to talk about something else.
I didn't bring you along to admire my ship.
Are you okay?
What's your problem?
I didn't mean to snap at you. What's wrong?
The silence wakes you up?
I find it rather peaceful. Don't worry, you'll get used to it.
You'll get used to it.
Sometimes we don't appreciate what we have until it's gone.
I don't have time to deal with your personal problems.
This ship's special.
Normally they're not.
Gathering information on us?
You're into ships?
That's not why you're here.
That was 300 years ago.
Let's change topics.
You sound down.
What's wrong?
Like I need this.
I'm sorry.
Good.
It's too quiet to sleep?
I like the silence.
It's not so bad.
I manage.
You're homesick.
Don't worry, Shepard. I know what's at stake. If we don't stop Saren, I won't have a home to go back to. I'll be ready when you need me.
Sounds like the Pilgrimage isn't just about finding resources for the fleet. Maybe it's about teaching you to appreciate your people and culture.
I need my crew to be in top form. I can't have you daydreaming about going home.
Maybe that's the point.
Stay focused.
Checking up on me, Shepard? Don't worry; I'm still here. But as soon as we stop Saren, I'm gone. My Pilgrimage can't wait forever.
Shepard, I need to talk to you. It's important.
You know the data you took from those geth control nodes? The information you uploaded to Alliance control? I want a copy of it.
Please! You don't understand what this could mean to my people!
Those files have information that could be vital to our efforts to understand the geth. It could be the key to helping us reclaim our homeworld!
Not right away. I'll stay with you as long as it takes to stop Saren. But my people need this!
Not right away. We will need to study it. It could take years. But it will give us new insight into how the geth have changed and evolved over the past centuries.
My people--I--owe you a great debt. One I can never repay.
The only thing I can offer in return is what you already have: my solemn promise to stay with you until Saren and his geth armies are defeated.
Thank you, Shepard.
Maybe even decades. But it's worth the time. This information will give us new insight into how the geth have changed and evolved over the past centuries.
Right. I'm sure the Alliance will have no problem turning it over to my people. Governments are always eager to work with the Migrant Fleet.
You're looking out for your own people. I understand that. I just wish it wasn't at my people's expense.
Don't worry. I'll still do everything I can to help you stop Saren. But as soon as this mission is over, I must resume my Pilgrimage.
You don't know my father. Stealing ships is a capital offense among my people. He'd probably want to execute us himself.
I hope you're right.
Good point. Was there something else you wanted to talk about?
That doesn't make me feel any better. Let's talk about something else.
That's true. I'm starting to wonder if that's what the Pilgrimage is really about. It's given me a whole new perspective on my people and our culture.
You're probably right. We quarians spend our whole lives traveling, but we really never leave home. The Pilgrimage has given me a whole new perspective on our culture.
You know, there's always a few who go on their Pilgrimages and never return. I always assumed something bad happened to them, but maybe they just wanted a different life.
I could never abandon my people, Shepard. I will go back eventually. But we have to stop Saren first. Otherwise, I might not have a home to go back to.
I'm sleeping much better now. I guess I'm getting used to how quiet your ship is.
I think I was a little homesick before. But I'm feeling much better now.
I still think a lot about my Pilgrimage, though. I know Saren's our top priority. But with all the worlds we go to, I was hoping to find something to bring back to the flotilla.
Yes, but it cannot just be some derelict ship my people can use for salvage. It has to be more than that. There's a lot expected of me.
I won't. You have my word on that. But I'm not going to just give up on my search. The Fleet needs the resources we find on our Pilgrimages.
Usually, people bring back something like a derelict ship we can use for salvage. But I need something bigger! There's a lot expected of me.
It's my father. He's the senior member of the Admiralty Board. He's one of only five people who can overrule the decisions of the Conclave for the good of the Migrant Fleet.
My father is responsible for the lives of seventeen million people -- our entire race is in his hands. And I'm his only child.
No, it doesn't work that way. My father's position isn't hereditary. I'll probably never serve on the Admiralty Board myself.
Officially, I'm just the same as any other citizen. But it doesn't work that way in practice. People have always treated me differently because of who my father is.
I probably had it easier than most growing up. But it's not all good. People like my father have enemies. And they're not above using me to get to him.
I know that! I wasn't saying...
See? This is why I don't tell people about my father. It always sounds like I'm bragging. Worse, it gives people this impression that I can never live up to!
My people place a high value on family and ancestry. There's an unspoken expectation that I'll live up to my father's example.
I guess I'm just tired of people judging me because of who my father is.
Everyone's waiting for me to do something great on my Pilgrimage. Something that will forever change our lives for the better.
If I don't, it's like I failed. And that reflects badly on both me and my father.
Yes... I know. But you have to understand quarian culture. We're a very insular society. The events beyond the flotilla don't much matter to the average citizen.
Our greatest dream is that one day, we'll return to our homeworld and drive out the geth. But even if we stop Saren, that's not going to happen.
There's still millions of geth behind the Veil. Until they're gone, our exile will continue.
Something that would help us better understand the geth. They've changed significantly since the exile; they've continued to evolve.
We've done our best to study them, but it's not easy. They're very reclusive. Until recently, they never went beyond the borders of the Veil.
And all the geth we run into now are under Saren's control. We'd need to find geth operating on their own. Independently.
But I don't want this to get in the way of our mission, Shepard. First, we stop Saren. Then I'll worry about my own problems.
Understood, Shepard.
You'll find the Conduit before he does. I know you will. You have to.
And after this is all over, when my Pilgrimage ends and I go back to my own people, I'll be proud to say I was a part of it.
You've been good to me. A lot of people treat quarians like second-class citizens. They just want us to go back to our fleet and disappear.
But you've treated me just like everyone else on your crew. Like an equal. That means a lot. And it says something about you.
Whatever happens, I just want to say thank you for that.
Yeah, I get that feeling, too. But I know you can handle whatever he throws at us. And I'll be right here if you need my help.
But you're the only one doing anything about it. You and your crew.
You took me on board and made me feel like I belonged. Not too many people would do that with a quarian.
That won't happen for a while yet. I'll be right here any time you need me.
Don't worry. You can always count on me.
Understood. I just had to get that out there. And I'm still right here if you need me.
When my people reach maturity, we leave our birth ships and seek acceptance with a new crew. It's necessary to maintain genetic diversity among the fleet.
Our lives aren't easy. Resources are scarce and we are constantly on the move. Everything we do must in some way contribute to the continuation of the Migrant Fleet.
I doubt I can tell you anything you don't already know. It's been almost three centuries since they drove my people into exile.
All I know is the story of their origins: what they were when we created them, and how they turned on us.
The geth were originally created to serve as an automated manual labor force. Initially, their intelligence was as limited as any VI.
Like what?
It wasn't easy growing up as the daughter of one of the Admiralty. Even before he joined the Board, he was a prominent figure. People looked to him for leadership.
Is something wrong?
Make it quick.
You want to bring this data back to the Migrant Fleet.
I can't pass out classified information.
If I give you this data, your Pilgrimage is over. You'll go back to your own people.
You think you can use this information to destroy your enemy.
Go ahead. Make a copy.
I never wanted anything more.
I'll be counting on you, Tali.
It'll take years to decipher and analyze the data.
Until our cryptologists decipher that data, it stays with the Alliance. After that, you can make an official appeal for access to the files.
I'm a soldier, Tali. I have to respect the chain of command.
Is this going to cause trouble later on?
Your father probably has some political pull, right? He wouldn't let them throw his little girl in jail.
We've got bigger problems than your father. Like Saren and the Reapers.
If they catch us, then Saren finds the Conduit. Whatever your father's got planned, I guarantee the Reapers will do worse.
The Normandy's the best ship in the fleet. They'll never catch us.
We've got bigger problems than the Council. Like Saren and the Reapers.
If they catch us, then Saren finds the Conduit. Whatever the Council's got planned, I guarantee the Reapers will do worse.
You do plan to return to the Migrant Fleet, right?
Good to see you smiling again. So to speak.
Why are you so cheerful?
We've still got a long way to go. You'll find something to take back.
What are you hoping to find?
You'd better not jeopardize my mission for the sake of your Pilgrimage!
What's so special about you?
So are you some kind of heir to the quarian throne or something?
You must get all kinds of special privileges.
If we don't stop Saren, the death toll's going to be a hell of a lot higher than seventeen million.
It must be tough on you.
Why didn't you tell me this before?
The work you're doing here is more important than anything any quarian has ever done before.
What would you need to bring back to make everyone happy?
Just remember why you're really here. Stay focused on Saren.
It won't be much longer. One way or another, it'll all be over soon.
If we don't stop him soon, it'll be too late.
We couldn't have done this without you, Tali.
Saren's still got a couple more surprises waiting for us.
Saren is looking to wipe out all life in the galaxy. Everyone's a part of this somehow, whether they know it or not.
I'm going to miss you when you go back to your own people, Tali.
I didn't bring you along as a favor, Tali. You're here because you contribute to the mission. And I need all the help I can get on this one.
This isn't getting us any closer to the Conduit.
Interesting.
I want to talk about something else.
What was your father like?
Of course.
What is it?
Don't waste my time.
I understand.
For your Pilgrimage.
Forget it.
Then you'll leave us.
By wiping the geth out.
It's encrypted.
I can't take that risk.
To kill the geth.
All right.
Take it.
Good.
That's enough.
Don't forget it.
All right.
Sorry. I don't have a choice.
I follow my orders.
Do we have a problem?
Wouldn't your dad help us?
Not a problem
Don't worry about that.
It doesn't matter.
Don't worry about that.
It doesn't matter.
But you're going back, right?
Glad you're feeling better.
You seem happy.
What's going on?
Don't worry. You will.
Like what?
Is that why you're here?
Why?
I don't have time for this.
You're royalty?
I'm responsible for trillions!
That's a lot of pressure.
I had no idea.
Preferential treatment?
I don't have time for this.
I don't have time for this.
I don't have time for this.
What if we save the galaxy?
We don't want that.
I don't have time for this.
So what's the answer?
I hope so.
We're getting close.
We better be.
An important part.
We haven't won yet.
This isn't about you.
You're welcome.
You earned it.
We're wasting time.
Tali's father
Tell me.
Let's change topics.
But no ship wants to accept someone who will be a burden on them. So, to prove our worth, we embark on a Pilgrimage.
We set out alone, leaving the flotilla and our families behind us. We only return once we have found something of value we can bring back to the fleet.
This is presented as a gift to the captain of the respective ship we wish to join. If the gift is accepted, we are welcomed into the crew.
That doesn't happen often. Most captains are eager to increase the size of their crew. It increases their own standing in our society.
Even when a gift is not particularly valuable, the captain usually accepts it out of a sense of tradition. However, there is a stigma to presenting a sub-standard gift.
It's not the best way to make a good impression on a new community. Most Pilgrims don't return until they find something worthwhile.
It's not like they just cast us out. Before we leave, we are given lessons in how to survive outside the flotilla, and given gifts to help us on our journey.
We also receive implants to fight off sickness and disease. Generations of living in an isolated and highly controlled environment have left our immune systems weaker than most.
By the time we leave the fleet, we are well-equipped for the Pilgrimage. This is a rite of passage for all quarians. If it were dangerous, our numbers would suffer.
Virtually every Pilgrimage ends with a triumphant return and the ritual presentation of the gift to one of the fleet's captains.
There are seventeen million quarians in the flotilla, and each of us relies on the others for survival. The bonds among my people are strong.
Unfortunately, we have had to surrender many of the freedoms and civil liberties other species take for granted.
Well, it's illegal for parents to have more than one child. If our population grows too much, it would strain our resources to their breaking point.
Of course, we also can't allow our numbers to become too few. If our population is in decline, the rule against single births is temporarily repealed.
In extreme cases of population decline, incentives are even offered to encourage multiple births. Though the Conclave hasn't had to take such measures in nearly a century.
The Conclave is our civilian branch of government. Each ship can elect a representative to serve on the Conclave and make decisions that affect the fleet as a whole.
On matters that affect an individual ship, however, the captain has the final say. It's a tradition that dates back to the early days when the fleet was governed by martial law.
Fortunately, most captains nowadays are smart enough to have an elected council from their crew to give them advice and guidance.
In practice. The Conclave and the respective council for each ship tend to set the rules that govern our daily lives. But in theory we are still under military jurisdiction.
The five top-ranking military officials in the fleet serve on the Admiralty Board. These five have the power to overrule any decision by the Conclave in case of emergency.
To do so requires unanimous agreement among the Admiralty. And they can only do this once. After that, the entire Board must resign their posts.
It's a safeguard that's served us well. In nearly three centuries, the Admiralty Board has only overruled the Conclave four times.
Over time, we made small modifications to their programming to allow them to perform more varied and complex tasks, bringing them closer and closer to true AI status.
This wasn't true AI research. We may have been skirting the bounds of the law, but we never did anything that was actually illegal.
The changes were so insignificant, so gradual, that we were able to control them. Or so we thought.
But one thing we underestimated was the power of the neural network. A million geth thinking simultaneously created an inherently unstable matrix.
Many of the geth's logic systems were designed to work in concert with other nearby geth. Basically, the more of them you have in a group, the smarter they are.
No, nothing like that. They cannot share sensory data or information. Their programming cannot handle that much simultaneous input.
Each geth maintains an individual awareness and identity. The neural network only operates on a process-based level. It's basically the synthetic equivalent of a subconscious.
But when they're in close proximity, they can coordinate low-level functional processes, freeing up more capacity for original or independent thought.
I'm probably over-simplifying. The geth are incredibly advanced and complex creations. All you need to know is that they get smarter when they gather in large numbers.
As we built more and more geth, their effective intelligence became more sophisticated, more abstract.
One day, a geth began to ask its quarian overseer questions about the nature of its existence. Am I alive? Why am I here? What is my purpose?
As you can imagine, this caused a near-panic among my people.
The geth were created to engage in mundane, repetitive, or dangerous manual labor. That's fine for machines, but it won't satisfy a sentient being for long.
The geth were showing signs of rudimentary self-awareness and independent thought. If the geth were intelligent, then we were essentially using them as slaves.
It was inevitable the newly-sentient geth would rebel against their situation. We knew they would rise up against us. So we acted first.
A general order went out across all quarian-controlled systems to permanently deactivate all geth. The geth responded to this order violently.
We had no other choice! The geth were already on the verge of revolution. By acting quickly, we had a chance to end the war before it began.
The hope was that most of the geth would still be little more than machines, incapable of organized resistance. But they had progressed much further than anyone anticipated.
The war was long and bloody. Millions upon millions of quarians died at their hands. In the end, we were forced to flee our own homeworld.
We feared the geth would pursue us, but they never came beyond the Veil. Now we drift through space, exiles searching for a way to reclaim what was once ours.
We made a mistake when we created the geth in the first place. But we didn't make a mistake when we went to war against them.
If we had not acted, they would have wiped us out! They're a synthetic life-form. They have no use for organics. None!
Why do you think they cut themselves off from the rest of the galaxy? Why do you think they've killed every organic being who's ever tried to contact them?
What does that tell you? The geth are not innocent victims in all this.
I'm sorry. I didn't mean to get so worked up. Most quarians tend to have pretty strong opinions about the geth.
You really think things would be any different if we'd waited for them to act first? The geth are not innocent victims in all this.
They're the enemy. They want to destroy us. Not just the quarians -- all organic life. That's why they've joined up with Saren. And that's why we have to stop him.
He had to set an example, and he expected the same of his daughter. Plus, he was pretty strict. A military man through and through.
He never allowed me to settle for anything less than excellence. As a kid, I sometimes felt like he was pushing me too hard.
But now I'm old enough to appreciate what he taught me. The world doesn't owe us anything. If we want something in life, we have to earn it.
Mother was around, but she always seemed to kind of blend into the background. Almost like she was overshadowed by my father. He tends to do that to people.
She passed on about five years ago. Some airborne virus that swept through the fleet. Happens sometimes when the filters start to break down.
I think my father took it pretty hard. After she was gone, he became even more focused on his work. I think that was his way of dealing with the grief.
Like I said, it wasn't easy. My father's not the kind of person you bond with. And he wasn't around all that much. Too busy.
People counted on him, and he took his duties seriously. Even when he was around, he always seemed a bit distant. Like his mind was always somewhere else.
Come to think of it, I can't ever remember seeing him smile. Not once. It's like he was always weighed down by all that responsibility.
I mean, I know he cares about me, but he never really showed it. Not in the usual way. I guess the best thing I can say about my father is that I respect him.
Can a captain choose to reject the gift?
I can't believe they just send you off alone.
What kind of freedoms?
That's your government?
So the ultimate power rests with elected officials?
How come the Council didn't step in and stop you?
You had to know it would blow up in your face.
So the geth share brain power?
So they're some sort of group consciousness?
That doesn't make any sense.
What made them rebel?
I don't see what's so bad about those questions.
What did you do?
You can't blame them for fighting for their survival.
You're the ones who started the war. The geth were just fighting for their survival!
You didn't really think they'd just let you destroy them without a fight, did you?
It's hard to feel sorry for you. Your ancestors tried to wipe out another species.
You got what you deserved.
They didn't kill Saren.
I didn't meant to offend you.
You make a good point.
You didn't give them a real good first impression.
Where was your mother in all this?
Sounds like a tough upbringing. You don't resent your father at all?
Do they always accept?
Sounds dangerous.
Like what?
The Conclave?
You're democratic?
Isn't AI research illegal?
That was a mistake.
The neural network?
Why did they turn on you?
Like a hive mind?
I don't get it.
Why?
What happened next?
They defended themselves.
It was your fault!
What did you expect?
They defended themselves.
Serves you right.
Not every one.
Sorry.
Okay, you're right.
I'm not surprised.
What about your mother?
Were you close to your dad?
